Mind you i was using a pair of old skyzones before i got the FPV goggles so as far as screens go i havent been able to compare them to hdo2's or those orcas that just came out. IMO heres what could be improved on them

1) HDMI out without needing the 700 dollar DJI controller that i have no use for other than hdmi out.

2) HDMI in so i could use them with liftoff or velocidrone.

3) The stock foam pads are shit and don't seal. Im waiting on some thicker pads dji just released to come in the mail that will maybe solve the problem.

4) They are fairly power hungry and will drain 3s 18650 packs i made to run them in about 20-30 minutes.

I fly it right out of my back yard which is just a normal lot for the suburbs 60' x 100' and the tinyhawk is perfect for that. I fly the 5" Immersion RC Apex from there too but for a beginner 5" is a lot for backyard flying. So, let's address these issues one at a time.

1) The way you're living will lead you to at least a low-level depression, if it hasn't already. Let's be clear - depression isn't just feeling sad. It is a loss of positive feeling, if not a partial numbing of all types of emotion. It is an inability to be fully engaged in life, and a blindness to the deeper meaning in what you do. When you reach this point, you will be much more susceptible to addiction, which can fuck up your life in ways you'd not imagine if you haven't experienced it. It can also lead you into heavy, debilitating, clinical depression if it gets bad enough. That will prevent you from purposefully achieving anything in life, and from enjoying anything you accidentally get in life.

But, if you're not already in a serious, debilitating depression that requires professional help and massive medication, there is a path out of it that is simpler (and more consistently effective) than most people would assume. Here it goes.

  1. Get physical exercise everyday. It doesn't have to be intense, just move and sweat for a while.

  2. Healthy consumption. Eat food close to it's natural state, paying particular attention to your consumption of healthy fats. Drink clean water. Breath clean air, as much as possible.

  3. Spend time in sunlight, every day that you can. It doesn't have to be a long time. Aim for at least 20 mins though.

  4. Actively engage with a healthy social circle. Got family that wasn't abusive? Give them a call. Got friends that are doing something with their lives? Do something with them. Don't have those? Join clubs/groups/classes/whatever that are working on projects or useful skills, and start building your circle there. Church is also good for this, if you're into that sort of thing.

  5. Be working on something that requires you to be better than you are. Start a project that requires you to gain more skills than you currently have. Build something that requires you to obtain more knowledge. Develop something that requires practice.

  6. Stop dwelling on the past. I'm not saying you should ignore the past. Learn from it and let it go. Easier said than done, I know, but make an active effort of it. Keep a journal of what you've learned from the past events you dwell on, and then when an event stops being useful, replace your dwelling on it with something else. Find yourself thinking about it? Go work on a project, or call a friend, or workout. Having trouble doing that? Meditation works wonders for gaining some control over your mind. There are plenty of resources for meditation online, but if you want to try it and don't know where to start, DM me. I'm no teacher, but I have been meditating for ~20 years, and can point you to what works for me.

I know some of these don't sound appealing. But these are natural parts of a healthy human structure, and most people will enjoy them once they really have them. That should address the first problem. Now...

2) What should you do for a job? Once you have problem one fixed and your personal life/mental health is in order, life will start to feel meaningful... in certain contexts. Some things will be enjoyable, others won't. Please note- I'm talking about actual enjoyment, not just distraction from pain or numbness. Some areas of life will seem like a priority, others won't. The healthier your mind is, the clearer this distinction is.

I might be able to list specific jobs or qualifications that could make you some money, and might not suck. But, if you spend 8 hours a day doing something that, at best, "doesn't suck", and just for money... well, is that the life you want? If you know what is enjoyable and meaningful to you, you will know the area of life you want to engage in. And we live in a world that is now so varied in ways to make money, that someone who puts in the effort can get paid to do work related to almost any subject. Some people get rich playing videogames, for god's sake.

Find the meaning of your life. Find the thing that is such a priority to you and your relationship to the world, that you want to engage with it. Find the thing that you'd not only spend 40 hours a week on, but you'd happily spend 80 hours/week if that's what it takes. Develop some ideas on how to get paid for it. Then work on it. Work hard. Toss aside ideas that didn't work and develop ideas that are working. Put in the time and effort.

I can't tell you what that will be. It doesn't have to be magical to anyone else. It could be the trades that will inevitably be suggested here - they build and contribute to a community, and you may find that this is your engaging priority. It may be something that takes you back to school for years. Or it may be something nobody's done before. Dunno.

But when your mind is unfucked, your life starts to get unfucked. When your life is unfucked, you can see the best of what lies in front of you. When you know specifically where you want to get, you can start realistically plotting a course there.

This was more vague than you wanted, but I hope it was helpful.
